seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July to mid-September, once Andrews Pass is snow-free and before autumn storms close in on the 18-mile approach

June.reason: Snow still buries Andrews Pass and the upper Andrews Creek trail, turning the 18-mile approach into a multi-day snow slog.

July.reason: The pass usually melts out by mid-month and the rock dries, but mosquitoes are heavy at the lakes and early July can still hold snow.

August.reason: Approach is fully snow-free and the granite is dry; late-summer wildfire smoke in the Pasayten is the main thing that can spoil a trip.

September.reason: Cooler days and fewer bugs make the long approach easier; larches around the Cathedral Lakes turn gold late in the month.

October.reason: Short days and the first snowfalls can glaze the cracks and bury Andrews Pass, and a storm leaves you a long way from the car.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July to mid-September, after the approach slabs melt out and seeping corners dry, while SR 20 is open

June.reason: SR 20 is normally open, but snow can linger on the approach talus and upper ledges, and some corners still seep after the melt.

July.reason: Snow clears from the climbers' path and the wall dries through the month; early July can still leave wet streaks on the upper pitches.

August.reason: Dry rock and a snow-free approach; the wall is short from the road, so a hot day can be dodged with an early start.

September.reason: Settled weather, cooler temps and dry corners; larches around Cutthroat Lake turn late in the month and the trailhead gets busier.

October.reason: The highway usually stays open, but cold, short days and early snow can ice the ledges and make tree-anchored raps unpleasant.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through August, when the Southern Pickets approach basins and the Barrier are mostly melted out and weather is most stable

June.reason: Deep snow still covers Terror Basin and the high traverse, avalanche runout fills the gullies, and the ridge rock is often wet or corniced.

July.reason: Snow recedes from the approach basins through the month; lingering snow slopes still need axe and crampons on the high traverse.

August.reason: The most reliable window for the multi-day Southern Pickets approach: snow bridges are gone or firm and the rock is dry.

September.reason: Stable weather and fewer bugs, but snow slopes turn to hard ice and moats open wider, making the basin crossings harder.

October.reason: Early snow on the ridge, short days and a long committing approach far from any road make a stand-alone attempt unwise.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July and August, when the block at the ridge junction is melted out and dry and Stevens Canyon Road is open

May.reason: Stevens Canyon Road usually opens near Memorial Day; before then the approach adds a road walk and the Roof's start can be snow-choked.

June.reason: Snow covers the gully above Snow Lake for easy cramponing and glissading, but a moat at the ridge junction can complicate the start.

July.reason: The block melts out and dries, so the 5.6 roof is clean; lingering snow may still ease the upper gully early in the month.

August.reason: Dry rock and a snow-free route; the approach is a loose scree and talus grind, and the gully chimney sheds rock onto parties below.

September.reason: Still dry and usually quieter, though afternoons shorten and the first autumn storms can wet the gully and chimney.

October.reason: Stevens Canyon Road closes with the first heavy snowfall, usually mid-month, and early snow can glaze the roof pitch.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July to mid-September, after the pitch-five dihedral dries and the upper gully snow thins

June.reason: The gully above Colchuck Lake still holds steep snow needing axe and crampons, and the pitch-five dihedral usually runs wet.

July.reason: The approach gully melts back through the month and the wall dries; early July can still leave the Scoop dihedral damp.

August.reason: Dry cracks and a mostly snow-free gully; the west face takes afternoon sun, so start early to avoid baking on the 5.11c crux.

September.reason: Cool, dry and stable, ideal friction for the sustained crack pitches; larches in the Enchantments draw big crowds to the trailhead.

October.reason: Cold rock, short days and early snow on the approach gully; the Enchantment overnight permit season runs until the end of the month.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late August through September, once the approach gully is scree and the south face has cooled

June.reason: SR 20 is usually open but the approach gully still holds snow and wants boots and crampons, and the face may be seeping.

July.reason: The gully melts to scree by mid-summer and the rock dries; the south face bakes in full sun, which is hard on an 11-pitch 5.12.

August.reason: Dry and reliable, but full-day sun on the south face is hot for sustained crimps; late August cools and water may still run near the base.

September.reason: Cooler temperatures on the south face give the best friction for the bouldery crux; water is still found near the base early in the month.

October.reason: The south face stays warm on clear days, but short daylight for 11 pitches and early snow in the loose gully add real risk.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July to mid-September, once the Aasgard-side gully melts back and the bolted face has dried

June.reason: Steep snow lingers in the approach gully from Colchuck Lake, and seepage from the melting snow above can wet the face's seams.

July.reason: The gully melts back and the face dries through the month, though early July can still bring snow on the scramble to the sandy ledge.

August.reason: Dry rock and a mostly snow-free approach; the west-facing wall gets afternoon sun, so hot days favour an early start on the 5.11+ seam.

September.reason: Cool, stable weather gives the best friction on the insecure crux; the Enchantments larch season brings heavy trailhead crowds.

October.reason: Cold rock, short days and early snow in the approach gully; overnight camping at Colchuck Lake still needs a permit through October.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July through mid-September, after the snow moat at the wall base melts and the approach gully is dry

May.reason: The south-tending approach gully is still an avalanche path, and deep snow below Pineapple Pass leaves a large moat at the wall.

June.reason: The snow slope to the pass makes a fast approach but needs an axe, and a moat up to several feet deep can guard the first pitch.

July.reason: The moat shrinks and the west-facing bolted pitches are dry; weekends get crowded as the South Face routes fill up.

August.reason: A snow-free approach and dry rock; loose rock on the crux pitch and parties converging near the summit are the main hazards.

September.reason: Still dry and quieter, though the approach talus is loose and shorter afternoons limit time for the summit scramble.

October.reason: Early snow and verglas can coat the unprotected scramble to the summit, and the approach gully starts loading with snow again.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July through mid-September, when the approach gully is snow-free and the North Ridge scramble is dry

May.reason: The approach gully below Pineapple Pass is still an avalanche path and the unprotected North Ridge scramble is snow-covered.

June.reason: Snow on the approach gully speeds travel but needs axe and crampons, and lingering snow on the North Ridge makes the scramble serious.

July.reason: The bolted pitches west of the large gully dry out and the 100 m North Ridge scramble loses its snow patches.

August.reason: Dry rock throughout; a snow-free approach means loose talus, and the route is a quieter choice than the crowded South Face.

September.reason: Dry and stable with fewer parties, though shorter days tighten the time for the long unroped scramble and descent.

October.reason: Early snow or verglas on the unprotected North Ridge scramble is dangerous, and the approach gully begins loading with snow.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through early September, after Sibley Creek melts out and while the glacier descents still have firm bridges

June.reason: Avalanche debris fills Sibley Creek, steep snow guards the pass, and the loose ridge crest is still corniced or snow-plastered.

July.reason: The trail to Sibley Pass is usually snow-free by July; snow patches remain on the ridge, and glacier bridges below are still strong.

August.reason: The ridge is dry enough for the loose 5.6 R crux, and the Eldorado and Triad glaciers are in workable late-summer shape.

September.reason: Settled weather, but the glaciers bare off and open crevasses, making the descent toward Eldorado slower and more complex.

October.reason: Short days and first snows on exposed, loose 4th-class terrain; the Sibley Creek slopes start to load again with avalanche snow.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July and September: the Blue Lake basin is melted out and the west-facing cracks are dry, without August's hottest afternoons

May.reason: SR 20 has usually just reopened, but the basin below the Liberty Bell group is still under deep snow and the cracks run with melt.

June.reason: SR 20 is open, but snow still fills the approach basin and seeps can wet the lower corners; expect axe work to reach the base.

July.reason: The basin melts out and the long crack corners dry; morning shade on the west face keeps the crux cool until late morning.

August.reason: Reliably dry rock, but the west face bakes in afternoon sun and late-summer wildfire smoke can settle over Washington Pass.

September.reason: Cooler afternoons make the sunny west face comfortable and the approach is snow-free, though days are noticeably shorter.

October.reason: Cold, short days and early storms can glaze the crux crack, and SR 20 may close for the season after the first major snowfall.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August to mid-September, once the snow is off Aasgard Pass and the scree traverse, while the braided creek still runs

June.reason: Aasgard Pass and the scree traverse to the base are usually still snow-covered, adding steep firm snow to an already loose approach.

July.reason: The pass melts out through the month and the creek at 7,250 ft runs strongly; early July can still hold snow on the traverse to the base.

August.reason: The approach is snow-free and the east face gets sun from early morning to early afternoon; late-summer wildfire smoke can drift in.

September.reason: Stable weather and cool temperatures suit the long pitches, though the creek on the pass can thin out and the face goes into shade earlier.

October.reason: The face loses its sun early and grows cold, the first snow can coat Aasgard Pass, and the season's overnight permit window ends Oct 31.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July to August, after the Kachess River ford drops from snowmelt and the south-side talus and chimney are dry

August.reason: The ford is at its easiest and the rock is dry, but the south-facing talus gets hot and late-summer wildfire smoke is possible.

September.reason: Cooler temperatures and a low ford suit the talus slog; late-season wildfire closures can shut the Mineral Creek Trailhead.

October.reason: The first snow can glaze the chimney and gully, days are short, and the wilderness season winds down after mid-October.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August to September, when the long Park Lakes approach is snow-free and the Kachess ford is low, before fall snow

June.reason: Snow still covers the high Park Lakes basin and Spectacle Point camp, and the Kachess River ford runs high with melt.

July.reason: The approach melts out through the month and the ford drops; early July can still hold snow patches on the west ridge.

August.reason: Snow-free approach, low ford and dry ridge rock make the multi-day trip most straightforward; wildfire smoke is possible.

September.reason: Cooler days suit the 16-mile round trip and the ford is at its lowest; late-season fire closures can shut the trailhead.

October.reason: The route has been climbed in mid-October, but an early storm can snow in the ridge, freeze camp water and shorten the days sharply.

November.reason: Snow typically covers the west face and Spectacle Point, and the long remote approach leaves little margin in short days.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July to August, once the base snowfield melts off the approach gullies and the east face warms in morning sun

September.reason: Still dry, but the east face goes into shade early and the thin slab and crack pitches feel cold in the afternoons.

October.reason: Short, cold days on a shaded face, possible verglas on the cracks, and SR 20 can close after the first major storm.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August to September, when snow has cleared the crest from the Tooth to Chair Peak and the rappel off Bryant is dry

September.reason: Cooler, stable weather and a fully melted crest; shorter days mean an early start to finish before dark.

October.reason: The first snow and verglas make the exposed 4th-class crest and loose rock treacherous, and daylight is short.

October.reason: Snow can dust the North Face and the long gravel roads to 6,760 ft may be snowed over, making the drive the crux.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: April to May, when the couloir snow is consolidated and days are long, before warm afternoons bring wet slides

January.reason: The couloir is firm and icy, the Cascade River Road is gated far below the trailhead, and short days make the long approach hard.

February.reason: Deep winter snowpack adds avalanche danger to the Cascade Pass crossing and the road approach is still long on skis.

March.reason: The snowpack begins to consolidate and days lengthen; persistent-slab and storm-snow danger still demand careful timing.

April.reason: Consolidated snow and long days, with the road gate higher up the valley; large wet slides off slopes near Hurry-up Peak on warm days.

May.reason: Firm morning snow and corn by midday; start early, as the couloir and the exit toward the col transition quickly to wet slides.

June.reason: Still in shape early, and the road usually opens to the trailhead late in the month, but moats open near Trapper Lake and snow softens.

July.reason: The couloir melts toward rock and rockfall, moats and thin snow bridges near the lake make the line largely out of condition.

September.reason: Rock stays dry but snow patches for water are usually gone, and shorter days make a 12-15+ hour traverse harder to finish.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July through September, when the sunny southwest wall is dry and the approach gully is snow-free

June.reason: The approach gully off the Blue Lake Trail can hold snow early in the month, but the sunny southwest wall dries fast once SR 20 is open.

July.reason: The wall is dry and the approach gully is melted out; midday sun on this southwest face gets hot, so start early or climb in the afternoon shade.

September.reason: Cooler temperatures suit the sustained 5.11 cracks while the southwest aspect still catches warming afternoon sun.

October.reason: The sunny aspect can stay climbable on clear days, but early snow and ice can coat the approach gully before SR 20 closes for winter.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-August through September, after the approach gully stops running water and before the autumn rains return

July.reason: The approach gully usually still has running water on the chossy waterfall step and small snow patches, making the fixed-line scramble slick.

August.reason: The approach gully typically dries out by early-to-mid August; the lichen and seepage on the roofs have had the most time to dry.

September.reason: Dry approach slabs and cooler temperatures for the sustained overhanging pitches; shorter days make a bivy or pre-dawn start more important.

October.reason: Autumn rain soaks the approach slabs and fixed lines, and freeze-thaw loosens rock on the upper pitches and roofs.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July through September, once the basin below Ellinor has melted and the basalt ridge is dry

May.reason: Snow still covers the ridge ledges and the connecting basin, with cornices and hidden creeks under the snow in the basin below Ellinor.

June.reason: A hanging snowfield and a steep snow finger below Ellinor remain, with weak snow bridges and a moat; ice axe and crampons are needed.

July.reason: Most of the basin snow has melted and the pillow-basalt ridge is dry; an axe may still help on the last snow finger early in the month.

August.reason: The ridge and basin are snow-free, but water sources dry up, so carry enough for the whole traverse over exposed class 4 ground.

September.reason: Snow-free and cooler, with shorter days; the first autumn rains make the fractured basalt and the loose downclimb slick.

October.reason: Rain and early snow make the loose gendarme downclimb dangerous, and short days leave little margin on the ridge.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August through September, after the residual avalanche snow at the base has shrunk and Squire Creek has dropped

June.reason: Avalanche debris usually buries the base, the Squire Creek ford runs high with snowmelt, and upper basin slabs are still shedding snow.

July.reason: Residual avalanche snow at the toe often leaves a moat to cross onto the rock, and the ford can still be high early in the month.

August.reason: The ford is low, the base is usually reachable, and east-facing rock gives morning sun and afternoon shade on hot days.

September.reason: Cool afternoons in the shade and a low creek; stay climber's right on the rappels to avoid the wet gully by the slab waterfall.

October.reason: Rain returns and the waterfall beside the route grows, making the descent gully wetter and the brushy approach slippery.

evidence: MP: base commonly buried under residual avalanche snow for much of the climbing season; east-facing, morning sun https://www.mountainproject.com/route/113865042/waterfall-buttress

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September, after the summit gully melts out and Copper Glance Creek drops

June.reason: The trail is snow-covered above about 5,500 ft, Copper Glance Creek runs high at the crossing, and the south gully is a steep snow climb.

July.reason: Snow lingers in the summit gully into July, so carry an ice axe; by late month the approach is snow-free and the creek is low.

August.reason: The gully is mostly melted to talus and scree, the basin camp is dry, and Forest Road 5130 is open; watch for rockfall in the loose gully.

September.reason: Stable, cool weather and larches in the Copper Glance basin; the gully is snow-free, though loose talus and rockfall remain.

October.reason: Early snow can return to the gully and the road may close with the first storms; days are short for the long talus descent.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July to mid-August, when the face is dry and the glacier snow bridge is still intact

June.reason: The two-day approach over Itswoot Ridge is still snow-covered, the creek crossings run high, and the granite cracks seep.

July.reason: The glacier is well bridged and the approach is melting out; the thin crux cracks can stay damp early in the month.

August.reason: Dry granite and long daylight; afternoon thunderstorms are common, and the snow bridge onto the glacier can melt out by late month.

September.reason: Snow bridges onto the glacier have often melted out, forcing a crevasse detour, and shorter days squeeze the long approach.

October.reason: Early storms can put snow on the face and the glacier, and cold days leave little margin on a remote multi-day objective.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July through August, when the approach and the snow traverse to the notch have melted and the ridge is dry

May.reason: SR 20 may only just have reopened; deep snow on the approach rib and basin, and Early Winters Creek runs high at the log crossing.

June.reason: Doable once dry, but expect a steep snow traverse to the notch at the route's start and wet lower pitches; bring an axe.

July.reason: The approach rib and basin melt out and the spring at the camp bench still runs; afternoon thunderstorms are the main hazard.

August.reason: Dry rock and a snow-free approach; the spring near the camp can run low, so carry water for a long linkup day.

September.reason: Cool, stable weather; shorter days make the Burgundy linkup tight, and the runout summit slab is best done before any freeze.

October.reason: Cold, short days and early snow on the ridge; SR 20 typically closes for winter in November and access ends with it.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August into September, once Squire Creek runs low for the ford and the slabs have dried out, before the fall rains return

June.reason: Snowmelt keeps the Squire Creek ford and the tributary crossing high and cold, and the slabs and grassy ledges often still seep.

July.reason: The creek drops and the basin clears of snow; early July can still bring a pushy ford and wet streaks on the lower pitches.

August.reason: Lowest creek levels and dry rock; the SSW-facing slab bakes by midday, so start early to climb the smearing pitches before the heat.

September.reason: Cooler temperatures suit the friction and finger-traverse pitches, and the ford stays low until the fall storms begin.

October.reason: Fall rain swells the creek and leaves the slabs slow to dry, short days tighten a long approach, and new snow can dust the upper basin.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August through September, once the high Boundary Trail and Sunny Pass melt out, with larch color near Sunny Pass late in September

June.reason: The high country around Sunny Pass is usually still snowed in, and the rough Iron Gate spur road may not yet be cleared of winter damage.

July.reason: Snow melts off the Boundary Trail through the month; early July can still leave drifts at Sunny Pass and on the summit slopes.

August.reason: Trail and summit scramble are snow-free; watch for late-summer wildfire, which can close the Iron Gate road and trailhead outright.

September.reason: Cool, dry days and larches turning gold around Sunny Pass and Horseshoe Basin late in the month; the first snow can arrive by month's end.

October.reason: Early snow can cover the exposed ridge and make the high-clearance spur road hazardous, and fall hunting season is busy on these roads.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September, once the Stuart Lake road is open and Aasgard Pass has a melted-out boot path, before fall snow

May.reason: The Stuart Lake road is usually still gated, adding miles, and Aasgard Pass is a full snow climb with spring avalanche and cornice risk.

June.reason: Aasgard and the col to the tower are snow climbs needing axe and crampons; the road usually opens but early-June snow on Aasgard can still slide.

July.reason: Snow on Aasgard recedes toward a boot path; the col often still holds firm snow, so bring an axe for the final approach and camp.

August.reason: Most snow is gone from Aasgard, the col can be reached on Class 2 rock, and the short 5.5 step is dry.

September.reason: Stable weather and fewer crowds, with larch season late in the month; the Enchantment permit lottery covers overnight trips through October.

October.reason: New snow and verglas on Aasgard Pass and the ridge, cold hands on the tricky crux protection, and short days for a long approach.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July and August, when the steep approach snowfield is softening by day but not yet bare ice, and Aasgard is melted out

May.reason: The Stuart Lake road is usually still gated and Aasgard Pass and the approach snowfield carry spring avalanche and cornice risk.

June.reason: Deep snow on Aasgard and a large, steep snowfield to the base; firm early-morning snow needs axe and crampons and can still slide.

July.reason: The snowfield to the west-side base is consolidated and softens by mid-morning for good kicked steps, and the chimney rock is dry.

August.reason: Aasgard is a boot path and the rock is dry; the shrinking snowfield turns firmer, so time the crossing for softened snow.

September.reason: Settled weather, but the remaining snowfield can be hard old ice by now, needing crampons or a detour on loose rock around it.

October.reason: New snow on icy old snow makes the crossing to the base hazardous, and cold, short days squeeze a long approach.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August into September, when the trailless approach slopes and wall ledges are free of snow and the lichen-covered rock is dry

June.reason: SR 20 is open, but snow and ice linger on the steep off-trail approach benches and on ledges on the wall at over 6,000 ft.

July.reason: The approach benches melt out and ledges dry through the month; early July can still leave wet streaks and snow patches at the base.

August.reason: Dry rock for the thin, runout pitches; late-summer wildfire smoke from the Methow can settle over Washington Pass.

September.reason: Cool, stable days suit the thin crux climbing, and the approach is dry; nights turn cold late in the month.

October.reason: Cold rock and early snow on the ledges and descent, with short days, until the North Cascades Highway closes for winter.
